323.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
323.hook: exiles hang up their harps and ask how to sing in a strange land
323.howItsDone: Many Jews say Psalm 137 before Grace after Meals on weekdays, and at many weddings 'If I forget thee, O Jerusalem' is recited or sung just before the groom breaks a glass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song for the Sabbath and the palm tree. Your line was flourish like a palm. Were you sweet and strong today? Now, a much sadder song. Day three hundred twenty-three.

Anyone who's moved far from home knows the feeling. You're doing fine. You've got a job, friends, a routine. Then one day you hear a song from back home, or smell a dish your grandmother made, and it hits you in the chest. Homesickness. Now imagine that home was destroyed, and you were marched away to a foreign empire. Two and a half thousand years ago, that happened to the people of Judah. And one of them wrote a song about it that's still sung, and still quoted at every Jewish wedding.
screen: `A SONG FROM BACK HOME.` → `HOMESICKNESS IN THE CHEST.` → `MARCHED AWAY TO BABYLON.`

segments.voice: In 586 before the common era, the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple, and carried many of its people off into exile. Psalm one thirty-seven is their song. "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." On the willows there, they hung up their harps. And their captors, the psalm says, asked them for entertainment: sing us one of the songs of Zion. And they answer with a question. How can we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land? It's a question every exile asks. Can you keep your faith, your music, your self, far from the place it belongs? Then comes the oath: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Let my hand lose its skill, let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I don't remember you, if I don't set Jerusalem above my highest joy. That oath became part of Jewish life. At many weddings, just before the groom breaks the glass, someone says these words: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem. At the happiest moment, a memory of loss. The psalm doesn't end gently. Its last lines are a cry of fury at the people who destroyed their city, so raw that it's hard to read. The Psalms don't hide that grief can turn into rage. They put it into words and bring it before God, rather than acting it out. And the harps? They didn't stay on the willows forever. Jews went on singing in every foreign land they came to.
screen: `586 BCE: JERUSALEM FALLS.` · `HARPS ON THE WILLOWS.` · `HOW CAN WE SING HERE?` · `THE OATH AT EVERY WEDDING.` · then, large: `IF I FORGET THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with homesickness. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you miss, or a time, or a person. A childhood home. A city. A grandmother's kitchen. A version of yourself. Let the missing come up. Don't push it away, and don't drown in it. Just sit beside it, the way the exiles sat by the river. Then ask: what from that place can I still carry here? A song, a habit, a way of being. If you pray, you can bring your longing to God. The bell holds the time.
By the rivers of Babylon. Psalm one thirty-seven: exiles who wept, hung up their harps, and swore never to forget Jerusalem.
screen: `BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: if I forget thee. Today, remember one place or person you've lost, on purpose, and let them into a happy moment. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
324.hook: a cry from the deep, said in the days before Yom Kippur
324.howItsDone: In many communities, Psalm 130 is said aloud in the morning service during the Ten Days of Repentance between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and many people recite it in times of trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon, the exiles' song. Your line was if I forget thee. Did you remember someone on purpose? Today, another cry from a low place. Day three hundred twenty-four.

Most of us have had a night like it. Three in the morning, awake, staring at the ceiling. Something has gone badly wrong, or you've done something you regret, and it feels like you're at the bottom of a well. Too far down for anyone to hear. Everything polite has fallen away. What comes out, if anything comes out, isn't a speech. It's a cry. There's a psalm for exactly that place, and it's only eight verses long. Today: Psalm one thirty.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE BOTTOM OF A WELL.` → `NOT A SPEECH. A CRY.`

segments.voice: Psalm one thirty is one of fifteen psalms with the heading Song of Ascents. The Mishnah describes fifteen steps in the Temple where the Levites stood and sang, and many connect these songs to those steps, or to pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem. This one climbs from the very bottom. It opens: "Out of the depths" have I called You, O Lord. In Hebrew, mi-ma'amakim. The depths of the sea, the pit, the lowest place. And Hasidic teachers love a second reading: not only from my deep trouble, but from deep inside me. A prayer from the bottom of the heart, where nothing is fake. Then the psalm makes an honest admission. If You kept a record of every wrong, Lord, who could stand? But with You there is forgiveness. It doesn't pretend to be innocent. It asks for mercy. And then the most beautiful image in the psalm: my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning. Yes, more than watchmen for the morning. Picture a guard on the night shift, staring east, waiting for the first gray light. Then he knows the night is over. The psalm repeats the line, like someone saying it twice because it's that long a night. That's why, in many communities, this psalm is said every morning in the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Those are days for honest accounting. And they're said from the depths, waiting for the light.
screen: `A SONG OF ASCENTS.` · `MI-MA'AMAKIM: FROM THE DEPTHS.` · `WHO COULD STAND?` · `WATCHMEN WAITING FOR MORNING.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one honest cry. Settle, and breathe. Go down, gently, to the lowest place in you right now. Something you're sorry for. Something you're afraid of. Something you need. Don't dress it up. Find the fewest words that say it. Maybe just: help. Or: I'm sorry. Or: I'm scared. Say it inside, once, from the bottom. Then wait, the way a watchman waits for the morning. If you pray, you can say it to God. The bell holds the time.
Out of the depths. Psalm one thirty, a cry from the lowest place, and from deep inside, said in the days before Yom Kippur: my soul waits, more than watchmen for the morning.
Your line: out of the depths. Today, if you find yourself in a low place, say one honest word from there, and wait for the morning. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: Unto the mountains (Psalm 121)
325.hook: "He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep"
325.howItsDone: Many Jews recite Psalm 121 before travel, at a sickbed and for protection in childbirth; it is often printed on cards or plaques placed near a newborn, and it is part of the Shabbat afternoon psalms in some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one thirty, a cry from the depths. Your line was out of the depths. Did you say one honest word from a low place? Today, we look up. Day three hundred twenty-five.

Think about the last time you were watching over someone through the night. A sick child. A parent in the hospital. A friend on the couch after a terrible day. You try to stay awake, and sooner or later your head drops. Nobody can keep watch forever. We all sleep. That's exactly the thought behind one of the most beloved psalms, often said for travelers, for newborns, and for anyone who needs protecting. It starts with a person looking at the mountains. Today: Psalm one twenty-one.
screen: `WATCHING OVER SOMEONE AT NIGHT.` → `YOUR HEAD DROPS.` → `NOBODY CAN KEEP WATCH FOREVER.`

segments.voice: It's another Song of Ascents, one of the pilgrim songs. Picture a traveler on the road to Jerusalem, looking up at the hills ahead. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" The mountains are beautiful, and they're also where danger hides on a long journey. And the answer comes straight back: my help comes from the Lord, maker of heaven and earth. Not from the mountains. From the One who made them. Then the psalm's great promise: "Behold, He that keepeth Israel doth neither slumber nor sleep." The Hebrew word is shomer: a keeper, a guard, a watchman. It's the word for someone on the night shift, the one who keeps watch while others rest. In just eight verses, forms of that word appear six times. The Lord is your keeper. He'll keep you from all evil. He'll keep your going out and your coming in, from now and forever. The sun won't strike you by day, nor the moon by night. That's why Jews say this psalm for protection: before a journey, for a woman giving birth, at a sickbed. It's often printed on cards hung near a newborn's crib. And Hasidic teachers found a hidden reading in the opening question. From where, me-ayin, can also be heard as from ayin, from nothingness. Help comes out of the moment when you admit you have nothing left. Someone is keeping watch when you can't.
screen: `EYES LIFTED TO THE MOUNTAINS.` · `HELP FROM THE MAKER OF HEAVEN.` · `SHOMER: THE KEEPER.` · `ME-AYIN: FROM NOTHING.` · then, large: `HE DOESN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a hill or the horizon. If you can see one from where you are, a hill, a skyline, the edge of the sky, look at it. If not, close your eyes and picture a range of mountains far off. Settle, and breathe. Lift your eyes, literally. Notice how different it feels to look up and out instead of down. Ask the psalm's question quietly: where will my help come from? Think of the people you're watching over. Picture them kept, even while you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's promise. The bell holds the time.
Unto the mountains. Psalm one twenty-one: I lift my eyes and ask where help will come from, and the answer is a keeper who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
Your line: he doesn't sleep. Tonight, when you put down the worries you're keeping watch over, let someone else hold the night shift. Day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Psalm 27 in Elul
326.hook: said through the month before the High Holy Days: wait for the Lord, be strong
326.howItsDone: From the start of Elul through the High Holy Day season, many communities add Psalm 27 to morning and afternoon or evening prayers, and Ashkenazi communities blow the shofar each weekday morning of Elul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one twenty-one and the keeper on the night shift. Your line was he doesn't sleep. Did you let someone else hold the night? Day three hundred twenty-six.

Athletes have a preseason. Actors have rehearsals. Before a wedding there are weeks of fittings and planning and nerves. Nobody walks into the big day cold. The Jewish year works the same way. Before the High Holy Days, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's a whole month of warming up. It has its own sounds: the shofar blown in the morning. And its own psalm, said every day, twice a day in many communities. Today's word is the name of that month: Elul.
screen: `A PRESEASON, A REHEARSAL.` → `NOBODY WALKS IN COLD.` → `A MONTH TO WARM UP.`

segments.voice: Elul is the last month of the Jewish year, the month right before Rosh Hashanah. It's a month for turning around, teshuvah, getting ready to stand before God. Tradition hears a hint in its four letters: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. They're the first letters of a line from the Song of Songs: ani le-dodi ve-dodi li, I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. So Elul isn't only a time of fear. It's a time of closeness. And every day of Elul, many communities add Psalm twenty-seven. It opens with courage: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" An old midrash reads the psalm as a map of the season ahead. My light: that's Rosh Hashanah. My salvation: that's Yom Kippur. And later, when the psalm says God will hide me in His shelter, the Hebrew word is sukkah: the festival of Sukkot that comes after. The psalm goes through the whole holiday season. But it's honest, too. The middle of the psalm gets shaky. Hide not Your face from me. Even if my father and mother leave me. It isn't the voice of someone who has it all together. And then the last line, the one Elul hangs on: "Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let thy heart take courage; yea, wait thou for the LORD." Wait, then be strong, then wait again. Getting ready isn't about having answers. It's about staying, with courage, until the day comes.
screen: `ELUL: THE MONTH BEFORE.` · `I AM MY BELOVED'S.` · `LIGHT, SALVATION, SHELTER.` · `WAIT, BE STRONG, WAIT.` · then, large: `WAIT, AND BE STRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm twenty-seven once. If you can, find it, and read it slowly, all fourteen verses. Notice where it's brave and where it trembles. If you can't, sit with its first and last lines. Settle, and breathe. The Lord is my light; whom shall I fear? Let one fear come up. Then the last line: wait, and be strong. You don't have to solve the fear today. Just wait beside it, with a little courage. If you pray, you can say the psalm as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Elul. The month before the High Holy Days: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine. Its psalm ends: wait for the Lord, be strong.
Your line: wait, and be strong. Today, when something big is coming and you feel unready, take one small step to prepare, and let your heart take courage. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Sow in tears (Psalm 126)
327.hook: sung before grace on Shabbat: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy"
327.carry: sow in tears, reap in joy
327.howItsDone: On Shabbat and festivals, many families sing Psalm 126, Shir ha-ma'alot, before Grace after Meals, often to lively tunes that everyone at the table knows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elul and Psalm twenty-seven. Your line was wait, and be strong. Did you take one small step to get ready? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

It's Friday night, or a festival afternoon. The long meal is over. Plates pushed back, a few crumbs of challah on the tablecloth, kids getting restless. And before the grace after meals, someone starts a song, and the whole table joins in, often loudly, often banging the table in rhythm. Shir ha-ma'alot. A Song of Ascents. It's one of the happiest songs in a Jewish home. And right in the middle of it are the words: sow in tears. Today: Psalm one twenty-six.
screen: `THE MEAL IS OVER.` → `THE WHOLE TABLE SINGS.` → `AND IN THE MIDDLE: TEARS.`

segments.voice: Psalm one twenty-six remembers a homecoming. When the Lord brought the exiles back to Zion, it says, we were like people dreaming. Our mouths filled with laughter, our tongues with song. Even the nations said: God has done great things for them. It's the other side of Psalm one thirty-seven, the rivers of Babylon. The ones who wept by the rivers come home, and it feels too good to be real. Then the psalm turns to a prayer: bring back the rest of us, like streams in the Negev, the southern desert, where dry riverbeds suddenly flood after rain. And then the farming picture: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." A farmer walks out weeping, carrying a bag of seed, and comes home with joy, carrying sheaves. Why weep while sowing? In a hard year, seed is food you're choosing not to eat. You're burying it in the ground on a hope. That takes grief and trust at the same time. You may remember a Talmud story about the dreaming line. Honi, the circle-maker, puzzled over how seventy years of exile could feel like a dream. He met a man planting a carob tree, which takes seventy years to bear fruit. Why plant it? My grandparents planted for me, the man said, so I plant for my grandchildren. That's sowing in tears. You may not eat the fruit. You plant anyway. So on Shabbat, full and happy, Jews sing about tears. Because the joy at the table grew from seeds someone once sowed, crying.
screen: `LIKE PEOPLE DREAMING.` · `STREAMS IN THE NEGEV.` · `SEED YOU CHOOSE NOT TO EAT.` · `HONI AND THE CAROB TREE.` · then, large: `SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant something with a hope. If you can, actually plant something today: a seed in a pot, a cutting in water, a bulb in the ground. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of something you're doing that's hard, and whose fruit you can't see yet. Raising a child. Healing. Learning. Saving. Rebuilding something broken. Picture it as a seed in the ground. Say, inside, what you hope it grows into. If you pray, you can ask for the harvest. The bell holds the time.
Sow in tears. Psalm one twenty-six, sung before grace on Shabbat: the exiles came home like dreamers, and they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Your line: sow in tears, reap in joy. Today, do one hard thing whose fruit you won't see yet, and do it anyway. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Psalms for the sick
328.hook: communities divide the whole book to read for someone who is ill
328.howItsDone: Jewish communities organize Tehillim groups that divide the Book of Psalms for someone who is ill, name them in the Mi she-berakh prayer at the Torah reading, and wish them refuah shlemah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one twenty-six, the song before grace. Your line was sow in tears, reap in joy. Did you do one hard thing whose fruit you can't see yet? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

The news comes into the group chat late at night. Someone's mother is in the hospital. It's serious. And within an hour, something happens that's become common in Jewish communities: a list appears. Psalms one to ten, Sarah. Eleven to twenty, David. Twenty-one to thirty, the Cohens. By the next evening, a whole community of people, some of whom have never met the sick woman, has read the entire Book of Psalms for her. Today: psalms for the sick.
screen: `A MESSAGE LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A LIST APPEARS.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK, FOR ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Saying psalms for someone who is ill is one of the oldest and most widespread Jewish customs. When there's nothing else to do, you can do this. Often it's shared: a group divides all one hundred fifty psalms, so the whole book gets said for one person, sometimes every day. The person is named in the Hebrew way, with their own name and their mother's: Sarah, daughter of Rachel. Some add a custom with the longest psalm, one nineteen, which is arranged by the Hebrew alphabet: they read the sections whose letters spell the sick person's name. Some psalms are especially loved for this. Psalm twenty: "The LORD answer thee in the day of trouble". Psalm thirty, a song of someone who cried out and was healed. And the prayer for healing goes back to the Torah itself. When Moses' sister Miriam became ill, Moses cried out five short words in Hebrew, one of the shortest prayers in the Bible: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." No long speech. Just her, and now. Jews also say a prayer called Mi she-berakh for the sick when the Torah is read, and wish each other refuah shlemah, a complete healing, of body and spirit. The psalms don't replace doctors. Jewish tradition values medicine deeply. And the Talmud teaches that visiting the sick is itself a kind of healing. But when you're far away, or it's three in the morning, or there's nothing left to try, a psalm is something you can hold, together.
screen: `A COMMUNITY DIVIDES THE BOOK.` · `NAMED WITH THEIR MOTHER'S NAME.` · `HEAL HER NOW: FIVE WORDS.` · `REFUAH SHLEMAH.` · then, large: `PSALMS FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a psalm for someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit. Picture their face. Say their name, quietly. If you can, find Psalm twenty or Psalm thirty and read it for them. If not, use Moses' five words: heal her now, or heal him now. Or just hold them in your mind with a wish for a complete healing. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Psalms for the sick. Communities divide the whole Book of Psalms to read for someone who is ill, and wish them refuah shlemah, a complete healing.
Your line: psalms for the sick. Today, reach out to one person who's unwell. A message, a visit, a psalm said for them. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: Everything that breathes (Psalm 150)
329.hook: the book ends: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD"
329.howItsDone: Psalm 150 is said every morning as the last of the psalms of praise (Pesukei de-Zimra), and many repeat its final verse to mark the end of the Book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, psalms for the sick, and a community reading the whole book for one person. Your line was psalms for the sick. Did you reach out to someone unwell? Today, the last psalm of all. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Think about how a great concert ends. Not quietly. The band brings everything in at once. Drums, horns, guitars, the crowd singing along, the lights all on. The last song is the one where nobody holds anything back. The Book of Psalms ends the same way. After a hundred and forty-nine songs of joy and grief, fear and hope, exile and homecoming, the very last psalm is pure, loud, everything-at-once praise. And its final line is about something you're doing right now. Breathing.
screen: `THE LAST SONG OF THE CONCERT.` → `EVERYTHING AT ONCE.` → `THE LAST LINE: BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Psalm one fifty is short, only six verses, and almost every line starts the same way: hallelu, praise. Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him for His mighty acts. And then the instruments pour in: praise Him with the blast of the shofar, with harp and lyre, with drum and dance, with strings and pipe, with loud cymbals, with crashing cymbals. It's the whole orchestra of ancient Israel, all at once. And then, the last line of the whole book: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Hallelujah. After all the instruments, the final one is breath. Not only priests or Levites or musicians. Every thing that breathes. Every person, every animal, anyone who can draw air. Jews say this psalm every morning, near the end of the psalms of praise that open the service, and many repeat that last line twice, to mark the end. The rabbis noticed something in the Hebrew. The word for breath, neshamah, is also the word for soul. And a midrash plays on it: read neshamah as neshimah, a single breath, and it says, for every single breath you take, praise God. Not once a day. Every breath. And so the Book of Psalms, and our two weeks of psalms, ends with breath. We began with a tree by the water, then the stars, the shepherd, the mountain, the open hand, a song for each day, Hallel, and Shabbat. This week: the rivers of Babylon, the depths, the mountains, Elul, sowing in tears, psalms for the sick, and now, everything that breathes.
